In the instant case, the following questions arose for consideration. They 
were: 
(a) Whether arbitration was validly invoked in the matter; 
(b) Whether the appointment of the arbitrators was in terms of the relevant 
clauses of the contract; 
(c) Whether Respondent | was aware of such invocation and consequential 
proceedings; and 
(d) Whether the Arbitral Tribunal was right in refusing to adjourn the 
proceedings and proceeding with the matter. 
Allowing the appeal, 
Held: 
In terms of the provisions of Clause 26(1) of the contract, the appellant 
vide letters dated 18-7-1991 and 2-9-1991 had requested the “engineer” to 
look into the disputes as raised by the appellant. These letters were admittedly 
received by NTPC. As stipulated in Clause 26(1) read with Clause 26(4), in 
the event of the “engineer” failing to notify his decision within 30 days after 
being requested, the party concerned would be within its rights to require that 
the matters in dispute be referred to arbitration. Since nothing was done with 
respect to the request made by the appellant within 30 days of the receipt of 
communication dated 18-7-1991 or even the one dated 2-9-1991, the appellant 
12


<!-- page 93 of 640 -->

Update_Vol. 3 
ARBITRATION ACT, 1940 — SECTION 28 
§17 
could validly require that the matters in dispute be referred to arbitration. Even 
assuming that in terms of the letter dated 28-11-1991, it was NPTC who was 
to be concerned with the matters in dispute, no appropriate decision was taken 
even within 30 days of this communication. In the circumstances, invocation of 
arbitration by the appellant vide its letter dated 20-3-1992 was perfectly valid 
and in terms of the contract. (Para 23.1) 
A copy of the letter dated 20-3-1992 addressed to NTPC was admittedly 
forwarded to and received by NPTC. Neither of them took appropriate and 
required steps in the matter within 60 days as contemplated by Clause 26.6.1 of 
the contract. In the circumstances, the step taken by the appellant to approach the 
Institution of Engineers (India) requesting its President to appoint the arbitrator 
in terms of said clause, vide its letter dated 7-7-1992 was also in keeping with 
the express terms of the contract. It is crucial to note that a telegram was sent on 
24-8-1992 on behalf of NPTC requesting the President, Institution of Engineers 
(India) to keep the action regarding appointment of arbitrator on their behalf in 
abeyance. It was stated that a detailed letter was to follow. However, nothing 
was done in the matter for more than a month and the detailed letter was never 
sent. In the circumstances, the President, Institution of Engineers (India) was 
absolutely right and justified in making the appointment of the second arbitrator 
on 29-9-1992. The appointment of the third arbitrator was in any case within the 
powers of the President. Thus, appointment of the second and third arbitrator 
and constitution of the Tribunal cannot be found fault with. (Para 23.2) 
The record is clear that NTPC was aware of the communications dated 18-7- 
1991 and 2-9-1991. If under the directions of the Government of India, NPTC 
was to take over matters including those related with the contract in question, 
NPTC ought to have been appraised of the issues in question by NTPC. In any 
case, the telegram dated 24-8-1992 as stated above, expressly shows complete 
awareness on part of NPTC and yet no further steps were taken by NPTC. 
No detailed letter as stated in the telegram was ever sent. Further, Respondent 
1 which is the successor-in-interest was made aware of the pendency of 
proceedings before the Arbitral Tribunal but chose not to appear and take part. 
Minutes of first two meetings of the Arbitral Tribunal were forwarded to and 
received by Respondent 1. Even telegrams seeking and granting adjournment 
of the proceedings were sent to Respondent 1. When in the meeting dated 7-4- 
1993 the schedule for days beginning from 20-4-1993 was fixed and copy of 
the minutes was sent to Respondent 1, the advocate for Respondent | addressed 
a letter to the arbitration on 9-4-1993. This letter not only indicates complete 
awareness of the proceedings but displays definite idea having crystallised 
to initiate appropriate proceedings in the High Court. If that be so, nothing 
stopped Respondent 1| from initiating such challenge, which never happened. 
The least that it could do in the circumstances was to be ready to participate in 
the proceedings and be ready on merits of the matter. However, even on 20-4- 
1993 i.e. eleven days after the letter was sent, it was not willing to participate. 
If it wanted adjournment in the matter, it ought to have consented to the 
extension of time as the Arbitral Tribunal had rightly indicated. The conduct of 
Respondent | as rightly commented by the Division Bench of the High Court, 
was extremely casual. (Para 23.3)

The Arbitral Tribunal in the present case had entered upon reference and 
held its first meeting on 13-1-1993. The mandate of Sections 28(1) and (2) 
of the 1940 Act read with Schedule I, Clause 3 of the 1940 Act is that the 
statutory period to complete the proceedings and make the award was four 
months after entering on the reference. The minutes of the meeting dated 7-4- 
1993 show awareness that the period would expire on 12-5-1993. The law on 
the point is clear that in such circumstances, the enlargement of time could be 
possible if parties to the arbitration agreement consent to such enlargement. In 
the circumstances, if the Arbitral Tribunal insisted upon appropriate consent to 
extend the time, no fault could be found with. At the same time, if Respondent 
1 was not willing to give such consent, the Arbitral Tribunal had to go on with 
the matter and make the award within the statutory period. The Division Bench 
was not right in observing that the Arbitral Tribunal showed undue haste in the 
matter. (Para 23.4) 
Thus, the Division Bench was not right and justified in allowing the appeal 
and setting aside the judgment and order passed by the Single Judge. Therefore, 
the judgment and order passed by the Division Bench of the High Court is set 
aside and the judgment and order passed by the Single Judge of the High Court 
is restored. (Para 24). Electrical Mfg. Co. Ltd. vy. Power Grid Corpn. of India

— Interest Act, 
1978, S. 3 — Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, S. 31(7) 
(Paras 7, 8, 11 and 14 to 25) 
ONGC floated a notice inviting tender for the supply of 1200 metric tons 
(MT) of sodium carboxy] methyl cellulose (CMC). Reliance Cellulose Products 
Ltd. (Reliance) submitted its tender quoting a price of Rs 14,999 per MT for 
quantities above 900 MT. The offer of Reliance was accepted for the supply of 
1200 MT of CMC, and accordingly, a supply order dated 1-12-1988 was placed 
on Reliance. Since Reliance agreed to supply 1200 MT only if the price is 
higher than Rs 14,999 per MT, the parties ultimately went to arbitration in order 
to decide what should be the contract price for supply of 1200 MT of CMC. A 
separate order, referred to as the repeat order, was also placed for supply of 600 
MT of CMC. The supply was made on time and payments were received for 
both contracts @ Rs 14,999 per MT. 
In October 1990, the petitioner filed a special civil application before the 
Gujarat High Court in the course of which, by an order dated 11-10-1990, the 
disputes between the parties were referred to arbitration, which were with regard 
to the price for the supply of 1200 MT and 600 MT of CMC respectively. 
By an award dated 29-12-1993, the arbitrators fixed the price of 1200 MT 
at Rs 18,500 per MT, and Rs 20,500 per MT insofar as 600 MT of CMC was 
concerned. The arbitrators awarded pre-reference, pendente lite and future 
interest all @ 18% p.a. Objections were filed to the award by ONGC. The 
15


<!-- page 96 of 640 -->

§18 
ARBITRATION ACT, 1940 — SECTION 29 
SC-Arbi. 
learned Civil Judge, by his judgment dated 30-7-1998, rejected these objections, 
but ultimately reduced the interest for all three periods to 10% p.a. 
The appellant contended that no good reason was given for reducing interest 
from 18% to 10%. The only reason that was forthcoming from the impugned 
judgment was that interest has been reduced because ONGC is a public sector 
undertaking. According to the appellants, therefore, pre-reference, pendente 
lite and future interest at 18% all become payable from the date of the cause of 
action till 21-1-1999, when ONGC had deposited an amount of Rs 1,09,34,323, 
and an amount of Rs 46,86,138 on 30-4-2003, on account of principal and 
interest @ 10% p.a., and differential interest till date. 
The respondents contended that though the plea that no pre-reference or 
pendente lite interest was payable, there is an express bar to the grant of such 
interest between the parties, was noted by both the learned Civil Judge and the 
High Court, but no finding had been given thereon. 
Clause 16 of the General Conditions of Contract between the parties is set 
out hereinbelow: 
“16. Our standard terms of payment are within 30 days of receipt of stores 
and inspection at site. But any delay in payment will not make the Commission 
_liable for any interest.” 
The issue involved in this appeal was whether the arbitrators could have 
awarded pre-reference, pendente lite and future interest all @ 18% p.a. under 
the Arbitration Act, 1940 i.e. whether Clause 16 amounted to a contractual bar 
to the payment of any interest on the facts of this case? 
Allowing the appeals, 
Held: 
Under the 1940 Act, in the absence of an express bar under the agreement, 
the arbitrator has jurisdiction to award interest for all three periods i.e. pre- 
reference, pendente lite as well as future interest. (Para 7) 
Ordinarily, a person who has a legitimate claim is entitled to payment within 
a reasonable time and if the payment has been delayed beyond reasonable 
time he can legitimately claim to be compensated for that delay whatever 
nomenclature one may give to his claim in that behalf. If that be so, it would 
be justified in placing a strict construction on the term of the contract. (Para 8) 
Under Section 3 of the Interest Act, 1978, it is clear that pre-reference 
interest can be allowed by an arbitrator unless there is a bar by virtue of an 
express provision between the parties. (Para 11) 
Section 31(7) of the new Act by using the words “unless otherwise agreed 
by the parties” categorically clarifies that the arbitrator is bound by the terms of 
the contract insofar as the award of interest from the date of cause of action to 
the date of award. Therefore, where the parties had agreed that no interest shall 
be payable, the Arbitral Tribunal cannot award interest between the date when 
the cause of action arose to the date of award. (Para 14) 
The conclusion of the Court that Engineers-De-Space-Age, (1996) 1 SCC 
516 had been overruled by Sayeed Ahmed & Co., (2009) 12 SCC 26 is incorrect 
for two reasons: first, a Bench of two learned Judges cannot overrule a coordinate 
Bench of two learned Judges; and second, the Court in Sayeed Ahmed case was 
16


<!-- page 97 of 640 -->

Update_Vol. 3 
ARBITRATION ACT, 1940 — SECTION 29 
§18 
not deciding a case arising under the 1940 Act, but was deciding a case arising 
under the 1996 Act. (Para 16) 
In a situation where the award passed by the arbitrator granting interest from 
the date of the award till the date of payment is not modified by the court, the 
effect would be as if the court itself had granted interest from the date of the 
decree till the date of payment. (Para 17) 
Section 31(7) of the Act (1996 Act), by using the words “unless otherwise 
agreed by the parties”, categorically specifies that the arbitrator is bound by the 
terms of the contract so far as award of interest from the date of cause of action 
to date of the award is concerned. Therefore, where the parties had agreed that 
no interest shall be payable, the Arbitral Tribunal cannot award interest. (Para 
18) 
It would depend upon the nature of the ouster clause in each case. In case 
there is express stipulation which debars pendente lite interest, obviously, it 
cannot be granted by the arbitrator. The award of pendente lite interest inter alia 
must depend upon the overall intention of the agreement and what is expressly 
excluded. (Para 19) 
Where the agreement expressly provides that no interest pendente lite shall 
be payable on amount due, the arbitrator has no power to award interest. In 
case there is nothing in the arbitration agreement to exclude jurisdiction of the 
arbitrator to entertaining claim for interest, the jurisdiction of the arbitrator to 
consider and award interest in respect to all periods is subject to Section 29 
of the Act. On the basis of principles of Section 34 the arbitrator would have 
the power to award pendente lite interest also. The arbitrator has the power to 
award interest. (Para 20) 
Grant of pendente lite interest may depend upon several factors such as 
phraseology used in the agreement, clauses conferring power relating to 
arbitration, nature of claim and dispute referred to arbitrator and on what 
items power to award interest has been taken away and for which period. If 
the contract expressly bars the award of interest pendente lite, the same cannot 
be awarded by the arbitrator. The bar to award interest on delayed payment by 
itself will not be readily inferred as express bar to award interest pendente lite 
by the Arbitral Tribunal. (Para 21) 
Under the 1940 Act, an arbitrator has the power to grant pre-reference 
interest under the Interest Act, 1978 as well as pendente lite and future interest. 
However, he is constricted only by the fact that an agreement between the 
parties may contain an express bar to the award of pre-reference and/or pendente 
lite interest. Since interest is compensatory in nature and is parasitic upon a 
principal sum not having been paid in time, the Supreme Court has frowned 
upon clauses that bar the payment of interest. It has therefore evolved the test 
of strict construction of such clauses, and has gone on to state that unless there 
is a clear and express bar to the payment of interest that can be awarded by an 
arbitrator, clauses which do not refer to claims before the arbitrators or disputes 
between parties and clearly bar payment of interest, cannot stand in the way of 
an arbitrator awarding pre-reference or pendente lite interest. (Para 24) 
In the present case, Clause 16 of the General Conditions of Contract only 
speaks of any delay in payment not making ONGC liable for interest. There is 
ay

§19 
ARBITRATION ACT, 1940 — SECTION 29 
SC-Arbi. 
nothing in this clause which refers even obliquely to the arbitrator’ s power 
to 
grant interest. Clause 16 cannot possibly interdict the payment of pendente lite 
interest on the facts of the present case. (Para 25) 
Clause 16 is not at all attracted inasmuch as factually there was no delay in 
payment as a sum of Rs 14,999 per MT had, in fact, been paid for both 1200 
MT and 600 MT, but that the balance only became payable on and from the 
date of the award. It is nobody’s case that there was delay in payment on the 
facts of this case. It is only after Reliance went in a writ petition before the 
High Court that it became clear that a higher price would be payable, which 
was left to the arbitrator to determine vide the High Court’s judgment referring 
the issue of price to an arbitrator, which was accepted by ONGC. In this view 
of the matter, it is clear that no delay on account of the higher price ever took 
place as it became payable only on and from the date of the award, Rs 14,999 
per MT having been paid on time earlier. This being the case, it is clear that 
even if Clause 16 were to have application, both pre-reference and pendente lite 
interest are not barred. (Para 26) 
The only reason given for reducing interest from 18% to 10% being that 
ONGC is a public sector undertaking, would not suffice to set aside what was 
within the arbitrator’s discretion. There is no finding that this discretion has 
been exercised perversely, given the interest rates at the time of the award. 
(Para 27). Reliance Cellulose Products Ltd. v. ONGC Ltd., (2018) 9 SCC 266:

[21] — S. 29 — Interest on claimed amount — Principles governing 
award of interest, summarised — Held, interest can be awarded (a) for pre- 
reference period, and (b) pendente lite, provided there is no express prohibition 
against the same in the contract — Further, said matter is within discretion of 
arbitrator to be decided on facts and circumstances of each case — In present 
case, initial claim dated 7-3-1986 was only in respect of price escalation —

claimant entitled to interest from date of subsequent claim (i.e. with effect 
from 20-4-1987) till date of award (i.e. 
31-7-1997) and thereafter from date of 
decree of trial court until payment realisation — However, on facts, said award 
of interest modified from 18% to 12% p.a. 
The Assam State Electricity Board (Board) entered into an agreement with 
Buildworth (P) Ltd. (claimant) for supply and installation of a circulating 
water piping system for Bongaigaon Thermal Power Station. The total value of 
purchase agreement was Rs 86.82 lakhs. A ceiling of Rs 9.16 lakhs was fixed 
under the escalation clause. The period of completion of contract was 12 months 
but it got delayed even beyond the extended date permitted to the claimant. The 
sole arbitrator awarded a sum of Rs 10,73,969 on account of idling charges of 
labour and machinery and towards price escalation. In addition, a lump sum of 
Rs 20 lakhs as interest was awarded between 7-3-1986 and 31-12-1997. Future 
interest was awarded @ 18% p.a. on the sum awarded, after a period of three 
months from the date of the award. The High Court by the impugned order 
upheld the award except in respect of award of interest. The High Court held 
that Section 29 of the Arbitration Act, 1940 did not confer jurisdiction on the 
19


<!-- page 100 of 640 -->

§21 
ARBITRATION ACT, 1940 — SECTION 29 
SC-Arbi. 
arbitrator to award interest prior to date of reference. Hence, present appeals 
were filed both by the Board and the claimant. 
The Board submitted that the claimant was not entitled to any price escalation 
beyond the ceiling limit of Rs 9,16,825 lakhs fixed under the escalation clause. 
And that the escalation clause applied only to the specific period of contract 
that is 12 months. Contesting the claim of idling charges on labour and 
machinery, the Board further alleged that the claimant also contributed to delay 
in completion of the project. 
The finding of the arbitrator was that there was much delay in completion of 
work of about 2 to 3 years. And that though there was no formal extension of 
time, the claimant was given informal extension of time. And that the contract 
is silent regarding the consequences of delayed completion. And that even if 
the Board did not give any formal extension of time, it did not object to such 
delay nor did it invoke the penalty clause. The arbitrator further noted that 
when the claimant specifically intimated the Board that the escalation provision 
in contract would not be applicable to extended period, the Board did not raise 
any objection and allowed the claimant to carry on the work. 
Dismissing the appeal of the Board and allowing the claim of interest for 
pre-reference period and thereafter but at a reduced rate of 12% p.a., 
Held : 
The next aspect of the matter relates to the award of interest for the period 
from 7-3-1986 to 31-12-1997. The arbitrator awarded a lump sum of Rs 20 
lakhs for a period of 11 years. The High Court set aside the award of interest on 
the ground that Section 29 of the Arbitration Act, 1940 contemplates the award 
of interest only from the date of the decree. The issue as to whether interest 
could be awarded for the pre-reference period and pendente lite under the Act 
of 1940 is not.res integra. (Para 21) 
In G.C. Roy, (1992) 1 SCC 508, a Constitution Bench of the Supreme Court 
held that where the agreement between the parties does not prohibit grant of 
interest and where a party claims interest and that dispute (along with the 
claim for principal amount or independently) is referred to the arbitrator, he 
shall have the power to award interest pendente lite. This is for the reason that 
in such a case it must be presumed that interest was an implied term of the 
agreement between the parties and therefore when the parties refer all their 
disputes-or refer the dispute as to interest as such — to the arbitrator, he shall 
have the power to award interest. This does not mean that in every case the 
arbitrator should necessarily award interest pendente lite. It is a matter within 
his discretion to be exercised in the light of all the facts and circumstances of 
the case, keeping the ends of justice in view. (Para 21) 
The Constitution Bench judgment in N.C. Budharaj, (2001) 2 SCC 721 
affirmed the power of the arbitrator to award interest on sums found due and 
payable for the pre-reference period, in the absence of a specific stipulation or 
prohibition in the contract to claim or grant such interest. (Para 22) 
The basis on which the High Court set aside the award of interest is hence 
contrary to the decisions of the Constitution Bench. (Para 23) 
The learned counsel appearing on behalf of the Board, however, submitted 
that a claim for damages gets quantified upon an adjudication by the arbitrator. 
20


<!-- page 101 of 640 -->

Update_Vol. 3 
ARBITRATION ACT, 1940 — SECTION 29 
§22 
Hence, it was submitted that no interest could be awarded prior to the date of 
the award. Even this aspect of the matter is, in our view, no longer res integra. 
The arbitrator has power to grant interest on damages under Section 3(1)(b) 
of the Interest Act, 1978, from the date mentioned in this regard in a written 
notice claiming such interest. The position which prevailed prior to the Interest 
Act, 1978 (to the effect that interest on damages would be payable only after 
ascertainment of damages) has undergone a change after the enactment of the 
Act. Interest on damages could be claimed from the date of the written notice 
as contemplated in the law. (Para 24) 
‘ 
The judgments on the point have been considered in a decision of three 
Judges of the Supreme Court in Ambica Construction, (2016) 6 SCC 36 in the 
context of a bar of jurisdiction to award interest for the period of the pendency 
of the arbitration under the 1940 Act if there is an express bar under the contract. 
The decision notes and affirms the powers of the arbitrator to award interest in 
the absence of a specific power or prohibition contained in the contract. (Para 
25) 
The contract in the present case contains no bar or prohibition against the 
award of interest. However, it has been submitted on behalf of the Board that 
the claimant was paid a sum of Rs 9,16,825 towards escalation, which was 
the amount contemplated under Clause 2.3.1 of the contract. However, as we 
have noted, this provision in the contract was correctly held by the arbitrator 
to apply only during the scheduled term of the contract and not in respect of 
the extended period. The respondent in its initial demands dated 7-3-1986 
and 23-4-1986 made claims on account of price escalation and submitted a 
consolidated bill on 9-6-1986. On 20-4-1987, the claimant addressed a legal 
notice, claiming a sum of Rs 10,73,416 together with interest 
@ 18% p.a. In 
the circumstances, upon the issuance of the above notice, the claimant was 
clearly entitled to claim interest with effect from 20-4-1987. The High Court 
was hence in error in setting aside the award of interest. (Para 26) 
In our view, having regard to what is stated above, the claimant is entitled to 
interest on the sum awarded from 20-4-1987 to 31-12-1997 and thereafter from 
the date of the decree of the trial court until payment or realisation. The rate of 
interest is, however, modified to 12% p.a., in respect of both the above periods. 
(Para 27). Assam SEB v. Buildworth (P) Ltd., (2017) 8 SCC 146: (2017) 4 SCC

in reversing award passed by arbitrator as affirmed by Single Judge of High 
Court — Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, S. 34 
The National Hydro-Electric Power Corporation (NHPC) had floated 
tender for certain work. This tender was awarded to Hindustan Steel Works 
Construction Limited (HSCL). As the contract between NHPC and HSCL 
permitted for sub-contracting of work, the said works were sub-contracted to 
the respondent. Subsequently, the respondent further sub-contracted this work 
to the appellant. Dispute arose between the appellant and the respondent over 
payment. The contract between them permitted reference of dispute to arbitrator 
under the provisions of the Arbitration Act, 1940. Hence, the matter was 
referred to the arbitrator. One of the core claims of the appellant was regarding 
revised rates of work. As per contract between HSCL and the respondent, it 
was specifically mentioned that HSCL would pay revised rates for carrying out 
work to the respondent. However, the agreement between the appellant and 
the respondent missed out this particular clause. Before the arbitrator it was 
specifically contended that the appellant was entitled for revised rates received 
by the respondent from HSCL. The arbitrator accepted this contention and 
passed the award. This award was affirmed by the Single Judge of the High 
Court. In appeal before the Division Bench, it was held that the respondent had 
no liability to pay revised rates. Hence this appeal. 
Dismissing the appeal, 
Held: 
When it is found that claim was entertained by the arbitrator on the basis of 
provisions in the contract entered into between HSCL and the respondent and 
the said provisions were not made applicable in the contract which was entered 
into between the appellant and the respondent, the approach of the arbitrator is 
clearly perverse in justifying the claim on the basis of provisions which were 
not even applicable. Whether contract entered into between HSCL and the 
respondent governed the relationship between the appellant and the respondent 
was a fundamental and jurisdictional issue and such an exercise is permissible 
by the court while examining the validity of an award. Undertaking this exercise 
did not amount to appraising the evidence or dealing with the matter as an 
appellate court. On the contrary, the approach taken by the Division Bench 
of the High Court is on the principle that an arbitrator is a creature of contract 
between the parties and if he ignores the specific term of the contract, it would 
be a question of jurisdictional error which can be corrected by the court. A 
deliberate departure or conscious disregard of the contract not only manifests 
the disregard of his authority or misconduct on his part, but it may tantamount 
to legal mala fides as well. It is further settled in law that the arbitrator is not 
a conciliator and cannot ignore the law or misapply it in order to do what he 
thinks just and reasonable. (Paras 13 and 14) 
Though the respondent has been able to get the benefit of enhanced rate 
in respect of Items 1 and 6 and is able to retain the same thereby depriving 
the appellant to get this benefit. However, in a matter of contract where the 
parties have to stick to be governed by the provisions of the contract entered 
into between them, equity has no role to play. Insofar as the contract between 
the appellant and the respondent is concerned, the appellant was satisfied with 
“escalation” clause. The respondent, while entering into contract with HSCL 
25

SC-Arbi. 
ensured that enhancement of rates by the principal employer i.e. NHPC in favour 
of HSCL will enure to the benefit of the respondent PCL as well. The appellant, 
however, could not successfully negotiate this aspect with the respondent in the 
absence of any such clause/arrangement in the contract entered into between 
the appellant and the respondent. As the contract between the appellant and 
the respondent deals only with escalation, the appellant has to be satisfied with 
the same. (Para 15). Sharma & Associates Contractors (P) Ltd. v. Progressive 
Constructions Ltd., (2017) 5 SCC 743: (2017) 3 SCC (Civ) 225: AIR 2017 SC 
847: (2017) 172 AIC 75.

[29] — Ss. 30, 33, 13 and 15 — Role and obligations of arbitrator while 
deciding disputes — Principles summarised — Duty to decide disputes 
according to legal rights of parties — Award — Scope of interference 
with, by court — Reappreciation of evidence by court once award has 
been made rule of court — Permissible, when award is erroneous in law 
and amounted to misconduct by arbitrator — Arbitrator, held, cannot 
ignore law or misapply it, nor can he act arbitrarily, irrationally, capriciously 
or independent of contract while passing award — He is not a conciliator — 
Arbitrator has to decide disputes according to legal rights of parties and not 
according to what he may consider to be fair and reasonable — Also, it is the 
duty and obligation of courts to maintain purity of standards and preserve full 
faith and credit as well as to inspire confidence in the minds of litigants while 
adjudicating claims of parties under Arbitration Law — In appeal against 
award, High Court examined claims threadbare and set aside certain claims, 
and granted extra amounts with regard to certain other claims — Contention 
that High Court could not have appreciated evidence to arrive at a conclusion 
different from that of arbitrator — Tenability — Held, High Court rightly found 
fault with award since arbitrator neither examined claims made by contractor

§28 
with reference to evidence placed before him nor recorded a finding as to 
whether contractor in fact had suffered losses as claimed by him — Hence 
held, High Court rightly interfered with award which is erroneous in law and 
amounted to misconduct on part of arbitrator — Judgment of High Court, 
affirmed — Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, Ss. 34, 31, 35 and 37 
Dismissing the appeals, 
Held: 
The High Court has rightly held that the arbitrator is not a conciliator and his 
duty is to decide the disputes submitted to him according to the legal rights of 
the parties and not according to what he may consider to be fair and reasonable. 
The High Court has further rightly made observation in the impugned judgment 
that an arbitrator cannot ignore law or misapply it, nor can he act arbitrarily, 
irrationally, capriciously or independent of the contract while passing the award. 
The courts of law have a duty and obligation to maintain purity of standards 
and preserve full faith and credit as well as to inspire confidence in the minds 
of litigants while adjudicating the claims of the parties by resorting to alternate 
dispute redressal method of arbitration under the provisions of the Arbitration 
Act. (Para 15) 
The High Court with reference to the itemwise Claims 1(q), (b), (c) and 2(a), 
(b), (e), (f) and (g) examined the claims at threadbare in the backdrop of the 
legal position laid down by the Supreme Court with a view to find out whether 
the award passed by the arbitrator in allowing certain claims was required to be 
interfered with on the ground that the arbitrator has committed misconduct in 
passing the award. The High Court has examined the correctness of the above 
claims awarded at Rs 8,16,412 as loss of profits at 10% of the contract value 
against Claims 1(a), (b), (c) and 2(a), (b), (e), (f) and (g) by assigning reasons. 
(Para 16.1) 
In the impugned judgment, the reasons assigned by the arbitrator in allowing 
the said claims have been examined by the High Court with reference to the 
delay in handing over the sites of Godowns Nos. 10 and 11 to the contractor and 
locations of some structures which were changed after the work was awarded. 
The award of the above items of claims in favour of the contractor is found fault 
with by the High Court for the reason that the arbitrator neither examined any of 
the claims made by the contractor under Claims 1(a), (b), (c) and 2(a), (d), (e), 
(f) and (g) with reference to the evidence placed before the arbitrator nor has he 
recorded a finding as to whether the contractor in fact suffered losses as claimed 
by him in the aforesaid items of claims and as to whether the respondent NBCC 
was liable. Therefore, it is a finding of fact recorded by the High Court on the 
relevant aspect holding that the arbitrator did not record reasons regarding the 
delay in handing over the location of the sites in favour of the contractor and 
rightly held that mere delay in handing over sites will not entitle the contractor 
to claim damages unless it is established that the same is the consequence of 
breach committed by the other party. The said reasoning of the High Court on 
the above aspect of claims is perfectly legal and valid as it has assigned valid 
and cogent reasons in support of the said conclusions arrived at and rightly 
disallowed the claims. (Paras 16.2 and 16.4) 
Further, the High Court has rightly held that the award of any sum in addition 
to the contract amount does not arise as has been awarded by the arbitrator and

made the rule of the court, more particularly when the contractor did not claim

(Para 17) 
The reasons recorded by the High Court on the contentious issues while

[30] — Ss. 30 and 33 — Legal misconduct by arbitrator — Arbitrator, 
if had gone beyond or awarded claims contrary to terms of contract —

objections regarding legal misconduct filed, passed decree in terms of award

ARBITRATION ACT, 1940 — SECTION 30 
§30 
— Jurisdiction and approach of High Court in appeal — High Court’s enquiry 
should be confined to whether any legal misconduct is committed by arbitrator 
and if so, how and in what manner — High Court cannot act as if appeal arose 
before it directly against award — It cannot accordingly proceed to examine 
legality and correctness of findings of fact of arbitrator by re-appreciating 
evidence and on that basis conclude that arbitrator had gone beyond terms of 
agreement between parties — An objection, neither raised before arbitrator 
nor before trial court, but raised for first time before High Court should not be 
entertained — It can set aside a reasoned award only when reasons ascribed by 
arbitrator are perverse to the extent that no man with ordinary prudence could 
take such view or there is error apparent on record or award is based on wrong 
proposition of law — None of these grounds were made out in the present case, 
and arbitrator did not award beyond or contrary to terms of contract — Award 
restored — Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, S. 34 
The appellant contractor and the respondent State entered into agreements 
for execution of certain civil works. Subsequently, some disputes having arisen 
between the parties pertaining to completion of works, its nature, manner of its 
completion, non-payment of the appellant’s bills, etc., the parties by invoking 
arbitration clause contained in the agreements, approached the civil court for 
appointment of arbitrator and for making reference to him for adjudication of 
disputes. The request was accepted and accordingly, a retired Chief Engineer 
was appointed as the arbitrator and the disputes were referred to him. Consequent 
upon the reference the appellant filed six claims. The arbitrator by a reasoned 
award, allowed the appellant’s three claims and rejected the remaining three. 
The respondent filed objections under Section 30 of the Arbitration Act, 
1940 against the award. The civil court rejected the objections and passed a 
decree in terms of the award. The respondent preferred an appeal before the 
High Court which by examining facts of the case, held that the award was 
contrary to Clauses 26, 3(1) and 1(46) of the agreements and thus the arbitrator 
by travelling beyond the terms of the agreement had committed misconduct 
under Section 30. 
The question which arose for consideration by the Supreme Court in the 
present appeal was whether the High Court was justified in allowing the 
objections filed by the respondent (State) under Section 30 of the 1940 Act and 
thereby was justified in setting aside of the award passed by the sole arbitrator 
on the ground of “legal misconduct’? In other words, the question was whether 
on facts any case of legal misconduct on the part of the arbitrator is made out 
by the State under Section 30 of the 1940 Act for setting aside of the award. 
Allowing the appeal, 
Held : 
It is not possible to agree and uphold the approach and reasoning of the 
High Court. What is the jurisdiction of the court under Section 30 when it 
examines the question as to whether any case of legal misconduct on the part of 
an arbitrator in passing an award is made out or not has been the subject-matter 
of several decisions of the Supreme Court and remains no more res integra. The 
approach of the High Court is wholly against the law laid down by the Supreme 
Court in its earlier decisions. (Para 22) 
29


<!-- page 110 of 640 -->

§30 
ARBITRATION ACT, 1940 — SECTION 30 
SC-Arbi. 
It is now well settled that an award can be set aside only on the grounds 
specified in clauses (a), (b) and (c) of Section 30 of the 1940 Act and on no 
other grounds. Indeed this is clear from the opening words of Section 30 itself. 
A fortiori, 
a reasoned award cannot be set aside unless it falls in any of the 
three clauses (a), (b) and (c) of Section 30. The grounds such as inadequacy 
of reasons in support of an award, error committed by the arbitrator on facts, 
alternate and/or more plausible view could be taken than what is taken by the 
arbitrator, improper appreciation of evidence done by the arbitrator in recording 
any finding, etc. are not the grounds on which any award much less a reasoned 
award can be set aside. In other words, none of these grounds can be made the 
foundation for setting aside the award because they do not fall within the four 
corners of any of the three sub-clauses of Section 30. The High Court did not 
apply the law laid down by the Supreme Court while deciding the appeal and 
hence, committed a jurisdictional error. (Paras 25, 26 and 29.1) 
The arbitrator is a Judge chosen by the parties and his decision is final. The 
court is precluded from reappraising the evidence. Even in a case where the 
award contains reasons, the interference herewith would still be not available 
within the jurisdiction of the court unless, of course, the reasons are totally 
perverse or the judgment is based on a wrong proposition of law. An error 
apparent on the face of the records would not imply closer scrutiny of the merits 
of documents and materials on record. By purporting to construe the contract, 
the court could not take upon itself the burden of saying that this was contrary to 
the contract and, as such, beyond jurisdiction. If on a view taken of a contract, 
the decision of the arbitrator on certain amounts awarded, is a possible view 
though perhaps not the only correct view, the award cannot be examined by the 
court. (Paras 23 and 24) 
In the present case, the High Court virtually sat as an appellate court as 
if it was hearing the appeal arising out of the award little realising, rather 
ignoring, its well-defined jurisdiction in such matter and proceeded to probe 
into all factual issues arising in the case. It seems to have gone to the extent of 
permitting the State’s counsel to file some documents in appeal and then went 
on to examine the case on facts and eventually, held that the arbitrator had 
travelled beyond the agreement and hence, committed legal misconduct. It was 
not permissible in law. The High Court should have confined its inquiry to find 
out as to whether any legal misconduct was committed by the arbitrator and, if 
so, how and in what manner. It was, however, not done. (Paras 29.2 and 29.3) 
The High Court’s finding that the arbitrator passed an award contrary to 
Clause 26 and thereby travelled beyond the terms of the agreement which 
constituted a legal misconduct on his part is on the face of it, untenable in 
law for the reason, inter alia, that this objection was neither raised before the 
arbitrator nor before the trial court in the manner in which it was raised for the 
first time in the High Court. In any event, in the absence of any finding recorded 
by the arbitrator and the trial court, such issue could not have been gone into 
for the first time in appeal by the High Court. That apart, it has otherwise no 
substance on facts for the simple reason that it being a question of fact, the same 
could not be examined in appeal. (Para 29.4) 
The High Court failed to see that Clause 26 only prohibits the appellant from 
assigning the agreement to any third person and it, therefore, had nothing to do 
30


<!-- page 111 of 640 -->

Update_Vol. 3 
ARBITRATION ACT, 1940 — SECTION 30 
§31 
with the claims filed by the appellants. It was an admitted fact that the appellant 
did not assign the agreement to any third person. The finding of the High Court 
that the award was rendered bad because it was passed in contravention of 
Clause 26 of the agreement is, therefore, not legally sustainable in law. (Para 
29.5) 
The High Court further failed to see that there was no error apparent on the 
face of the record in the findings recorded by the arbitrator. (Para 29.6) 
The High Court also failed to see that the trial court had elaborately gone 
into all the factual issues and rightly did not find any substance in the objections 
raised by the respondent; and lastly, the award being a reasoned one (running 
into 36 pages) the reasoning of the arbitrator could not be said to be perverse to 
the extent that no man with ordinary prudence could take such view nor was any 
finding of the arbitrator against any provision of law or in contravention of any 
of the clauses of the agreement so as to constitute a case of legal misconduct on 
the part of the arbitrator within the meaning of Section 30 of the Act for setting 
aside an award. (Para 29.7) 
It is clear from the facts of the case that the claims made by the appellant 
were essentially based on facts. They were accordingly probed on oral and 
documentary evidence adduced by the parties, which resulted in partial success 
of three claims in the appellant’s favour and rejection of three claims. So far as 
the State is concerned, they did not pursue their counterclaim consequent upon 
its rejection by the arbitrator. (Para 33) 
Thus, there is no perversity in the arbitrator’s reasoning nor is there any kind 
of apparent error whether legal or otherwise in the award which may constitute 
a case of any legal misconduct on the part of the arbitrator empowering the 
Court to set aside the award by taking recourse to Section 30 of the Act. The 
reasoning and the conclusion arrived at by the arbitrator is one of the possible 
views which were capable of being taken by the arbitrator on the material 
brought on record and there is no legal ground to set aside the same. (Para 34).

[32] — Ss. 30 and 33 — Scope of S. 33 proviso — Misconduct of arbitrator 
— Adduction of oral evidence before court to prove legal misconduct 
of arbitrator — Permissibility — Held, no oral evidence is permitted to 
be adduced in court to prove legal misconduct of arbitrator since legal 
misconduct has to be apparent and proved from proceedings carried on 
before the arbitrator — Jn petition for making award rule of court, application 
filed seeking permission to examine arbitrator and calling General Manager/ 
employee of respondent as witnesses rejected by civil court holding that it does 
not sit in appeal over arbitration award and does not reappreciate the evidence 
— High Court, while rejecting examination of arbitrator, permitted respondent 
to examine its employee as a witness in the proceeding — Sustainability — 
Held, grounds on which petition filed by respondent to prove misconduct of 
arbitrator in conducting of arbitral proceedings do not pertain to personal 
misconduct or moral misconduct of arbitrator as they are on account of non- 
consideration of relevant documents, recording of minutes during arbitral 
proceedings, not granting adequate opportunity and violation of principles of 
natural justice by arbitrator — Since said grounds fall under legal misconduct 
of arbitrator, held, any kind of oral evidence or examination of any witness in 
court to substantiate stand of legal misconduct of arbitrator is not permissible 
— Further held, person urging legal misconduct of arbitrator has to satisfy 
court from the records of arbitral proceedings that there has been a legal 
misconduct on part of arbitrator as a consequence of which the award gets 
vitiated — Hence, judgment of High Court set aside to the extent of permitting 
examination of witness with liberty to respondent to advance arguments to 
establish ground of legal misconduct from arbitral proceedings — Arbitration 
and Conciliation Act, 1996, S. 34(2) — Words and Phrases — “Misconduct” 
and “Legal misconduct” 
Partly allowing the appeal, 
Held : 
In the present case, the issue centres around Section 30 of the 1940 Act. 
The assail does not pertain to personal misconduct or moral misconduct of 
the arbitrator, as the allegations centres around non-consideration of relevant 
documents, ascription of reasons of passing of the award which do not flow 
from the material on record and further the conduct of the arbitrator during the 
arbitral proceedings in recording of the minutes, but falls within the ambit and 
sweep of legal misconduct on the part of the arbitrator under Section 30. (Para 
8) 
Misconduct does not always have a moral connotation. To elaborate, it may 
not have any connection with the individual/personal conduct of the arbitrator. 
The said conduct would be in sphere of moral misconduct. As far as legal 
misconduct is concerned, as the authorities would demonstrate, the same must 
be manifest or palpable from the proceedings before the arbitrator. To elaborate, 
a person urging the ground of legal misconduct has to satisfy the court from the 
records of the arbitral proceedings that there has been a legal misconduct on 
the part of the arbitrator as a consequence of which the award gets vitiated. The 
question of adducing any kind of oral evidence to substantiate the plea or stand 
32


<!-- page 113 of 640 -->

ARBITRATION ACT, 1940 — SECTION 30 
§33 
or stance does not arise. It has to be shown from the proceedings carried on 
before the arbitrator and the evidence adduced before the arbitrator. Evidence 
cannot be adduced in court to substantiate the challenge on the score of legal 
misconduct. No discussion pertaining to moral misconduct is made as that is 
not the issue in the case at hand. (Para 19) 
In the instant case, the High Court has granted liberty to the respondent 
herein to examine its General Manager to substantiate its claim and further 
Opining that the said evidence should be considered within the parameters of 
Sections 30 and 33 of the 1940 Act. The parties have pressed their argument 
relating to legal misconduct. Both the parties have construed the order that the 
said liberty has been granted to establish the misconduct and precisely that 
is the subject-matter of challenge. Therefore, to substantiate a stance of legal 
misconduct on the part of the arbitrator, examination of any witness in court is 
impermissible. It is because it must be palpable from the proceedings and the 
Single Judge has already directed that the proceedings before the arbitrator to be 
requisitioned by the civil court. Least to say, it will be open for the respondent 
to establish the ground of legal misconduct from the arbitral proceedings. (Para 
20). Cochin Shipyard Ltd. v. Apeejay Shipping Ltd., (2015) 15 SCC 522: (2016)

[33] — Ss. 30(c), 14(2) and 17 — Setting aside an award — Permissible 
grounds for — Ground under S. 30(c) of Arbitration Act, 1940 that 
award is “otherwise invalid’’ — Meaning and scope of — Held, S. 30(c) of 
Arbitration Act, 
1940 does not attract principle of ejusdem generis so far as the 
term “otherwise invalid” used therein is concerned — Hence, ground under 
S. 30(c) that award is “otherwise invalid” is quite wide in amplitude — Court 
concerned can set aside an award on ground that it is invalid where on the face 
of the things it runs counter to a valid law prohibiting such an award or where 
the subject-matter of the award has been lawfully dealt with by a statutory 
authority or a court and it is no longer available for disposal in accordance 
with the award under consideration — Hence, held, family arrangements 
validly made resolving disputes between the parties, even post-award would 
prevail over the award — In present case, dispute arising in relation to family 
business among four sons of late ML i.e. AK, MK, RK and NK — Reference of 
matter to arbitrator was made by NK as per arbitration agreement — Award 
passed pursuant thereto — During pendency of reference, one company petition 
was filed by MK before Bombay High Court and another subsequent company 
petition was filed by RK before Rajasthan High Court — While petition seeking 
abovesaid award to be made rule of court was pending, said company petitions 
were disposed of in terms of amicable family agreements arrived at among 
parties concerned — Held, if parties settled their disputes amicably by an 
agreement, even post-award, such settlement/agreement will prevail in view 
of requirement of Arbitration Act that an award will acquire the status of 
decree only when it is made a rule of court after rejection of all objections 
— In this view of the matter, there was no hindrance in law in upholding the

family arrangements made before Rajasthan High Court as well as Bombay 
High Court — Said family agreements deserved to have pre-eminence over 
the award in question and could not be ignored or obliterated on account of 
pendency of the award still waiting to be made a rule of court — In such a

Words and Phrases — “Otherwise invalid” (Paras 42 and 43) 
The present appeals arose out of common facts and disputes between 
members of a larger family belonging to the branches of four sons of late 
ML, the family patriarch who died in 1961. ML’s four sons effected a de facto 
partition of the then existing three family businesses. The eldest son (Late) NK 
became in-charge of the family business in Rajasthan. The next brother (Late) 
AK got charge of the business at Delhi and the remaining two 1.e. RK and MK 
got charge of the business at Bombay. In 1964, the company of the said group at 
Bombay i.e. SG Motors (P) Ltd. (Bombay) expanded to establish a factory for 
manufacture of oxygen. RK looked after the oxygen division and the youngest 
brother MK looked after the motor division of the said company. Later, some 
friction arose between the family members. Consequently, an attempt was 
made for a family agreement for partition of all the family business consisting 
_ 
of four partnership firms and four companies, but it did not succeed because of 
differences. Thereafter, all the four groups entered into an arbitration agreement 
on 6-8-1984 and appointed one HK, a family friend as the sole arbitrator for 
effecting a partition of the family business under the control of four groups into 
four equal lots but with an understanding that the division would maintain the 
place of business of each group as it existed already. 
On 7-8-1984, NK filed the arbitration agreement with the arbitrator, who 
entered into reference on 18-8-1984 and made communications with the other 
three brothers. VK expired on 19-10-1984. During the pendency of the reference, 
MK filed a company petition bearing CP No. 128 of 1985 before the High Court 
of Bombay mainly seeking injunction against AK and RK in respect of shares 
and management of both the divisions of SG Motors (P) Ltd. (Bombay). 
The family members of AK and RK filed a petition under Section 33 of the 
Arbitration Act, 1940 before the Delhi High Court to challenge the existence 
and validity of the arbitration agreement dated 6-8-1984 but ultimately the 
High Court of Delhi permitted the arbitrator to make and publish the award. 
The award dated 3-12-1987 was filed with the High Court of Delhi and notice 
was issued to the parties. Objection to the award was filed by MK within time 
and beyond time by RK and also by SG Motors (P) Ltd. (Bombay). On the other 
hand, AK filed Suit No. 581-A of 1988 under Section 17 of the Arbitration Act, 
1940 in the High Court of Delhi to make the award a rule of the court. 
The Single Judge of the Delhi High Court took notice of subsequent 
developments in the company case at the Bombay High Court and in another 
Company Petition No. 6 of 1986 filed by RK in the High Court of Rajasthan 
and set aside the award by order dated 11-12-1996. The said order was upheld 
in appeal by the Division Bench vide the impugned order dated 5-10-2001 
(challenged in Civil Appeal No. 2763 of 2002).

On the basis of a successful bid, son of MK entered into an agreement with 
the Receiver and exercised right of management in terms of such agreement. 
Ultimately, the Bombay High Court vide order dated 6-7-1989 sanctioned the

AK opposed the aforesaid settlement Scheme before the Company Court as

The Bombay company case thus attained finality. 
Company Petition No. 6 of 1986 was filed by RK group on 6-8-1986 before

a Scheme of Reconstruction and 
Family Settlement was arrived at between persons representing three groups

Although MK was not a party to that Scheme, his interest received considerable

The orders of the Single Judge of the High Court of Rajasthan accepting

pending, on 20-2-1995, RS entered into a compromise and settlement with the 
other parties who were signatory to the family settlement. MK prayed for and 
was granted time to examine the terms of the aforesaid settlement. 
While the appeal preferred by MK was still pending before the Division 
Bench of the Rajasthan High Court, he and his group filed an additional affidavit 
on 14-8-1995 in Suit No. 581-A of 1988 before the High Court of Delhi for 
setting aside the award on the additional ground that AK had undertaken before

before the High Court of Rajasthan alleging that AK was guilty of contempt

1988 when he had undertaken to withdraw the same. The said contempt petition 
was dismissed opining that the non-compliance was on account of certain

circumstances and not wilful. The said order had been challenged in the present 
Civil Appeal No. 503 of 2001. 
The Division Bench of the High Court of Rajasthan had permitted VS (son 
of AK) to be transposed as appellant in Civil Special Appeal No. 30 of 1994 and 
hence the said appeal continued even after MK filed an application on 4-7-2000 
to withdraw that appeal. Ultimately, by the judgment and order dated 3-4-2002, 
the Rajasthan High Court allowed Appeal No. 30 of 1994 as well as Appeal No. 
24 of 1994 and remitted the matter again to the Company Judge to proceed in 
accordance with law, mainly because the Division Bench found a case of non- 
compliance with Section 391(1) of the Companies Act,1956. 
RS did not accept the Division Bench order and preferred a civil review 
petition pointing out that: (7) she had already compromised the matter by way 
of a subsequent Scheme and filed the compromise petition on 20-2-1995, (ii) 
the only non-signatory group i.e. MK group had subsequently accepted that 
compromise/settlement and had prayed for withdrawal of Appeal No. 30 of 
1994, and therefore (iii) when all the stake-holders had accepted the terms of 
settlement and family arrangement, there was no need of interfering with the 
order of the Single Judge. The review petition was however dismissed. Hence, 
the present Civil Appeal No. 3687 of 2006 was preferred by RS. 
Thus, the issues before the Supreme Court were: (i) whether the award under 
the Arbitration Act, 1940 which was yet to be made a rule of the court deserved 
implementation or preference was required to be given to the settlements 
finalised by the judgment of the Bombay High Court and the Rajasthan High 
Court which had been put to peril by the order of remand impugned by RS, and 
(ii) whether any good ground was available to the Delhi High Court under the 
provisions of Section 30 of the Arbitration Act, 1940 for invalidating the award 
and for refusing to make it a rule of the court in exercise of power under Section 
17 of the said Act. 
Dismissing Civil Appeals Nos. 2763 of 2002 and 503 of 2001, but allowing 
Civil Appeal No. 3687 of 2006 to the extent stated herein, 
Held : 
Clause (c) of Section 30 of the Arbitration Act, 1940 does not attract the 
principle of ejusdem generis so far as the term “otherwise invalid” used therein 
is concerned. That ground for setting aside the award is quite wide in amplitude 
and available to the court concerned if it finds that the award requires to be 
treated as invalid because on the face of the things it runs counter to a valid 
law prohibiting such an award or when the subject-matter of the award has 
been lawfully dealt with by a statutory authority or a court and it is no longer 
available for disposal in accordance with the award under consideration. Such 
a situation is only illustrative and has been enunciated in the light of facts 
obtaining in this case. (Para 42) 
In the light of the judgments highlighting the significance of family 
arrangement under Hindu Law, and considering the Scheme of the Arbitration 
Act, 1940 and the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, the Supreme 
Court is satisfied that the family arrangements made before the Rajasthan High 
Court in 1994 before the Company Judge and in 1995 before the Division 
Bench need to be protected and given pre-eminence over the award which is 
36


<!-- page 117 of 640 -->

ARBITRATION ACT, 1940 — SECTION 31 
§34 
yet not made the rule of the court. If the parties settle their disputes amicably by 
an agreement, even post-award, such settlement/agreement will prevail in view 
of requirement of the Arbitration Act that an award will acquire the status of a 
decree only when it is made a rule of the court after rejection of all objections. 
In that view of the matter, there is no hindrance in law in upholding the family 
arrangements made before the High Court at Rajasthan as well as the judgment 
of the Bombay High Court which has attained finality. They deserve to have pre- 
eminence over the award in question. When the courts having jurisdiction were 
allowed to proceed and decide the properties available at Bombay and record a 
family arrangement in respect of other matters in a company proceeding before 
the Rajasthan High Court, the judgments and orders in these proceedings cannot 
be ignored or obliterated on account of pendency of an award still waiting to be 
made a rule of the court. In such a situation, the award has to be set aside on the 
ground that it is otherwise invalid on the date it is being considered for being 
made a rule of the court. (Paras 43 and 42). Rajni Sanghi v. Western Indian

Arbitrator awarding claims of (a) price escalation charges, and (b) idling 
charges, therefore, upheld 
The Assam State Electricity Board (Board) entered into an agreement with 
Buildworth (P) Ltd. (claimant) for supply and installation of a circulating 
water piping system for Bongaigaon Thermal Power Station. The total value of 
purchase agreement was Rs 86.82 lakhs. A ceiling of Rs 9.16 lakhs was fixed 
under the escalation clause. The period of completion of contract was 12 months 
but it got delayed even beyond the extended date permitted to the claimant. The 
sole arbitrator awarded a sum of Rs 10,73,969 on account of idling charges of 
labour and machinery and towards price escalation. In addition, a lump sum of 
Rs 20 lakhs as interest was awarded between 7-3-1986 and 31-12-1997. Future 
interest was awarded @ 18% p.a. on the sum awarded, after a period of three 
months from the date of the award. The High Court by the impugned order 
upheld the award except in respect of award of interest. The High Court held 
that Section 29 of the Arbitration Act, 1940 did not confer jurisdiction on the 
arbitrator to award interest prior to date of reference. Hence, present appeals 
were filed both by the Board and the claimant. 
The Board submitted that the claimant was not entitled to any price escalation 
beyond the ceiling limit of Rs 9,16,825 lakhs fixed under the escalation clause. 
And that the escalation clause applied only to the specific period of contract 
that is 12 months. Contesting the claim of idling charges on labour and 
machinery, the Board further alleged that the claimant also contributed to delay 
in completion of the project.

The finding of the arbitrator was that there was much delay in completion of 
work of about 2 to 3 years. And that though there was no formal extension of 
time, the claimant was given informal extension of time. And that the contract 
is silent regarding the consequences of delayed completion. And that even if 
the Board did not give any formal extension of time, it did not object to such 
delay nor did it invoke the penalty clause. The arbitrator further noted that 
when the claimant specifically intimated the Board that the escalation provision 
in contract would not be applicable to extended period, the Board did not raise 
any objection and allowed the claimant to carry on the work. 
Dismissing the appeal of the Board and allowing the claim of interest for 
pre-reference period and thereafter but at a reduced rate of 12% p.a., 
Held: 
No apparent error on face of record — Arbitrator considered all relevant 
aspects — Though price escalation clause in agreement applied only to 
specific period in contract, arbitrator pointed out that in present case it would 
apply to extended period because the parties through their conduct permitted 
the belated performance of their reciprocal obligations — Price escalation in 
performing any contract is a normal incident in this age of inflation 
The contention of the claimant was that Clause 2.3(a)(i) applied only for the 
specific period mentioned in the purchase order and not for the extended period of 
the contract. According to the Board, a cap of Rs 9.16 lakhs was imposed under 
the above provision and no price escalation was permissible beyond it. (Para 11) 
The arbitrator has taken the view that the provision for price escalation would 
not bind the claimant beyond the scheduled date of completion. This view of 
the arbitrator is based on a construction of the provisions of the contract, the 
correspondence between the parties and the conduct of the Board in allowing 
the completionof the contract even beyond the formal extended date of 6-9- 
1983 up to 31-1-1986. Matters relating to the construction of a contract lie 
within the province of the Arbitral Tribunal. Moreover, in the present case the 
view which has been adopted by the arbitrator is based on evidentiary material 
which was relevant to the decision. There is no error apparent on the face of 
the record which could have warranted the interference of the court within the 
parameters available under the Arbitration Act, 1940. The arbitrator has neither 
misconducted himself in the proceedings nor is the award otherwise invalid. 
(Para 13) 
The view which has been adopted by the arbitrator is in fact in accord with 
the principles enunciated in the judgments of the Supreme Court. In P.M. Paul, 
1989 Supp (1) SCC 368, a Bench of two learned Judges of the Supreme Court 
has held that escalation is a normal incident arising out of gap of time in this 
inflationary age in performing any contract. The Supreme Court held that the 
contractor was justified in seeking price escalation on account of an extension 
of time for the completion of work. Once the arbitrator was held to have the 
jurisdiction to determine whether there was a delay in the execution of the 
contract due to the respondent, the latter was liable for the consequence of the 
delay, namely, an increase in price. (Para 14) 
The award comports with principles of law governing price escalation 
firmly established by the decisions of the Supreme Court. For these reasons, we

4. ARBITRATION AND CONCILIATION ACT, 1996 
[41] — Generally — Nature of 1996 Act, as exhaustive self-contained code 
— Implications that follow therefrom i.e. a negative import that only such 
acts as are mentioned in the Act are permissible to be done and acts or 
things not mentioned therein are not permissible to be done 
On 28-4-2014, an arbitration award was passed pursuant to Arbitration Rule 
125 of the Grain and Feed Trade Association (GAFTA) directing the appellants, 
who were the sellers, to pay the respondents, who were the buyers, a sum of 
US $846,750 together with compound interest 
@ 4% calculated at quarterly 
rests. In appeal, by an order dated 16-4-2015, the Appellate Tribunal directed 
the appellants to pay a sum of US $815,000 together with compound interest @ 
4% calculated at quarterly rests. 
An execution petition was filed under Section 48 of the Arbitration and 
Conciliation Act, 1996 (the Arbitration Act) on 29-6-2015 by the respondents 
before the District Court, Gandhidham-Kutch. On 7-3-2016, the appellants filed 
their objections to the said petition. By an order dated 11-11-2016, the High 
Court transferred the aforesaid execution petition to the Commercial Division 
of the High Court of Gujarat. 
On 8-8-2017, the High Court of Gujarat dismissed the objections that 
were filed by the appellants and allowed the execution petition filed by the 
respondents. Being aggrieved by this judgment, the appellants filed an appeal 
under the Commercial Courts, Commercial Division and Commercial Appellate 
Division of High Courts Act, 2015 (the Commercial Courts Act), which 
was dismissed by the impugned judgment dated 28-9-2017, stating that the 
43


<!-- page 124 of 640 -->

§41 
ARBITRATION AND CONCILIATION ACT, 1996 
SC-Arbi. 
Commercial Courts Act did not provide any additional right of appeal which is 
not otherwise available to the appellants under the provisions of the Arbitration 
Act. 
Sections 13 of the Commercial Courts Act, read as under: 
13. Appeals from decrees of Commercial Courts and Commercial 
Divisions —(1) Any person aggrieved by the decision of the Commercial 
Court or Commercial Division of a High Court may appeal to the Commercial 
Appellate Division of that High Court within a period of sixty days from the 
date of judgment or order, as the case may be: 
Provided that an appeal shall lie from such orders passed by a Commercial 
Division or a Commercial Court that are specifically enumerated under Order 
43 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (5 of 1908) as amended by this Act and 
Section 37 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996. 
(2) Notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being 
in force or Letters Patent of a High Court, no appeal shall lie from any order 
or decree of a Commercial Division or Commercial Court otherwise than in 
accordance with the provisions of this Act. 
Sections 50 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, read as under: 
50. Appealable orders.—(1) An appeal shall lie from the order refusing to- 
(a) refer the parties to arbitration under Section 45; 
(b) enforce a foreign award under Section 48; 
to the court authorised by law to hear appeals from such order. 
(2) No second appeal shall lie from an order passed in appeal under this 
section, but nothing in this section shall affect or take away any right to appeal 
to the Supreme Court.” 
The issue involved in this appeal was whether an appeal, not maintainable 
under Section 50 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, is nonetheless 
maintainable under Section 13(1) of the Commercial Courts, Commercial 
Division and Commercial Appellate Division of High Courts Act, 2015? 
Answering in the negative, whilst dismissing the appeal, 
Held : 
Section 13(1) of the Commercial Courts Act, is in two parts. The main provision 
is a provision which provides for appeals from judgments, orders and decrees of 
the Commercial Division of the High Court. To this main provision, an exception 
is carved out by the proviso. The primary purpose of a proviso is to qualify the 
generality of the main part by providing an exception. The proper function of a 
proviso is that it qualifies the generality of the main enactment by providing an 
exception and taking out as it were, from the main enactment, a portion which, but 
for the proviso would fall within the main enactment. (Para 13) 
The proviso goes on to state that an appeal shall lie from such orders passed by 
the Commercial Division of the High Court that are specifically enumerated under 
Order 43 of the Civil Procedure Code, 1908, and Section 37 of the Arbitration 
Act. It will at once be noticed that orders that are not specifically enumerated 
under Order 43 CPC would, therefore, not be appealable, and appeals that are 
44


<!-- page 125 of 640 -->

Update_Vol.3 
ARBITRATION AND CONCILIATION ACT, 1996 
§41 
mentioned in Section 37 of the Arbitration Act alone are appeals that can be made 
to the Commercial Appellate Division of a High Court. (Para 14) 
Thus, an order which refers parties to arbitration under Section 8, not being 
appealable under Section 37(1)(a), would not be appealable under Section 13(1) 
of the Commercial Courts Act. Similarly, an appeal rejecting a plea referred to 
in sub-sections (2) and (3) of Section 16 of the Arbitration Act would equally 
not be appealable under Section 37(2)(a) and, therefore, under Section 13(1) of 
the Commercial Courts Act. (Para 15) 
Where the special Act sets out a self-contained code, the applicability of the 
general law procedure would be impliedly excluded. (Para 17) 
Once it is held that the Arbitration Act is a self-contained code and 
exhaustive, then it must also be held, using the lucid expression of Tulzapurkar, 
J., that it carries with it “‘a negative import that only such acts as are mentioned 
in the Act are permissible to be done and acts or things not mentioned therein 
are not permissible to be done”. (Para 19) 
Section 50 is a provision contained in a self-contained code on matters 
pertaining to arbitration, and which is exhaustive in nature. It carries the negative 
import that appeals which are not mentioned therein, are not permissible. This 
being the case, it is clear that Section 13(1) of the Commercial Courts Act, 
being a general provision vis-a-vis arbitration relating to appeals arising out of 
commercial disputes, would obviously not apply to cases covered by Section 
50 of the Arbitration Act. (Para 20) 
However, the question still arises as to why Section 37 of the Arbitration 
Act was expressly included in the proviso to Section 13(1) of the Commercial 
Courts Act, which is equally a special provision of appeal contained in a 
self-contained code, which in any case would be outside Section 13(1) of 
the Commercial Courts Act. One answer is that this was done ex abundanti 
cautela. Another answer may be that as Section 37 itself was amended by the 
Arbitration Amendment Act, 2015, which came into force on the same day 
as the Commercial Courts Act, Parliament thought, in its wisdom, that it was 
necessary to emphasise that the amended Section 37 would have precedence 
over the general provision contained in Section 13(1) of the Commercial Courts 
Act. Incidentally, the amendment of 2015 introduced one more category into 
the category of appealable orders in the Arbitration Act, namely, a category 
where an order is made under Section 8 refusing to refer parties to arbitration. 
Parliament may have found it necessary to emphasise the fact that an order 
referring parties to arbitration under Section 8 is not appealable under Section 
37(1)(a) and would, therefore, not be appealable under Section 13(1) of the 
Commercial Courts Act. (Para 21) 
In all arbitration cases of enforcement of foreign awards, it is Section SO 
alone that provides an appeal. Having provided for an appeal, the forum of 
appeal is left “to the court authorised by law to hear appeals from such orders”. 
Section 50 properly read would, therefore, mean that if an appeal lies under 
the said provision, then alone would Section 13(1) of the Commercial Courts 
Act be attracted as laying down the forum which will hear and decide such an 
appeal. (Para 22) 
45


<!-- page 126 of 640 -->

§42 
ARBITRATION AND CONCILIATION ACT, 1996 
SC-Arbi. 
As no appeal lies under Section 50 of the Arbitration Act, no forum can be 
provided for. (Para 23) 
It is Section 50 that provides for an appeal, and not the letters patent, given 
the subject-matter of appeal. Also, the appeal has to be adjudicated within the 
parameters of Section 50 alone. Concomitantly, where Section 50 excludes an 
appeal, no such appeal will lie. (Para 25) 
Fhe matter can be looked at from a slightly different angle. Given the objects 
of both the statutes, it is clear that arbitration itself is meant to be a speedy 
resolution of disputes between parties. Equally, enforcement of foreign awards 
should take place as soon as possible if India is to remain as an equal partner, 
commercially speaking, in the international community. In point of fact, the 
raison d’Otre for the enactment of the Commercial Courts Act is that com- 
mercial disputes involving high amounts of money should be speedily decided. 
Given the objects of both the enactments, if we were to provide an additional 
appeal, when Section 50 does away with an appeal so as to speedily enforce 
foreign awards, we would be turning the Arbitration Act and the Commercial 
Courts Act on their heads. Admittedly, if the amount contained in a foreign 
award to be enforced in India were less than Rs | crore, and a Single Judge of 
a High Court were to enforce such award, no appeal would lie, in keeping with 
the object of speedy enforcement of foreign awards. However, if, in the same 
fact circumstance, a foreign award were to be for Rs 1 crore or more, if the 
appellants are correct, enforcement of such award would be further delayed by 
providing an appeal under Section 13(1) of the Commercial Courts Act. Any 
such interpretation would lead to absurdity, and would be directly contrary to 
the object sought to be achieved by the Commercial Courts Act viz. speedy 
resolution of disputes of a commercial nature involving a sum of Rs 1 crore and 
over. For this reason also, Section 13(1) of the Commercial Courts Act must 
be construed in accordance with the object sought to be achieved by the Act. 
Any construction of Section 13 of the Commercial Courts Act, which would 
lead to further delay, instead of an expeditious enforcement of a foreign award 
must, therefore, be eschewed. Even on applying the doctrine of harmonious 
construction of both statutes, it is clear that they are best harmonised by giving 
effect to the special statute i.e. the Arbitration Act, vis-a-vis the more general 
statute, namely, the Commercial Courts Act, being left to operate in spheres 
other than arbitration. (Para 27). Kandla Export Corpn. v. OCI Corpn., (2018)

[42] — Generally — Scope and purpose — Four pillars of foundation of 
the Act, explained 
46


<!-- page 127 of 640 -->

Update_Vol.3 
ARBITRATION AND CONCILIATION ACT, 1996 
§42 
Speedy conclusion of arbitration proceedings hardly needs to be emphasised. 
Commenting upon the structure of the English Arbitration Act, 1996, Mustill 
and Boyd in their Commercial Arbitration, 2001 companion volume to the 2nd 
Edn., have commented that this Act is founded on four pillars. These pillars are 
described as: 
(a) The first pillar: Three general principles. 
(b) The second pillar: The general duty of the Tribunal. 
(c) The third pillar: The general duty of the parties. 
(d) The fourth pillar: Mandatory and semi-mandatory provisions. (Para 14) 
The Indian Arbitration Act, 1996 is also based on the aforesaid four 
foundational pillars. First and paramount principle of the first pillar is “fair, 
speedy and inexpensive trial by an Arbitral Tribunal”. Unnecessary delay 
or expense would frustrate the very purpose of arbitration. Interestingly, the 
second principle which is recognised in the Act is the party autonomy in the 
choice of procedure. This means that if a particular procedure is prescribed 
in the arbitration agreement which the parties have agreed to, that has to be 
generally resorted to. It is because of this reason, as a normal practice, the Court 
will insist the parties to adhere to the procedure to which they have agreed upon. 
This would apply even while making the appointment of substitute arbitrator 
and the general rule is that such an appointment of a substitute arbitrator should 
also be done in accordance with the provisions of the original agreement 
applicable to the appointment of the arbitrator at the initial stage. However, 
this principle of party autonomy in the choice of procedure has been deviated 
from in those cases where one of the parties have committed default by not 
acting in accordance with the procedure prescribed. These were the cases where 
appointment of the independent arbitrator made by the Court in exercise of 
powers under Section 11 on account of “default procedure”. The present case, 
however, is concerned with the constitution of substitute Arbitral Tribunal 
where earlier Arbitral Tribunal has failed to perform. (Paras 15 and 16) 
In the case of contracts between government corporations/State-owned 
companies with private parties/contractors, the terms of the agreement are 
usually drawn by the government company or public sector undertakings. 
Government contracts have broadly two kinds of arbitration clauses, first 
where a named officer is to act as sole arbitrator; and second, where a senior 
officer like 
a Managing Director, nominates a designated officer to act as 
the sole arbitrator. No doubt, such clauses which give the Government a 
dominant position to constitute the Arbitral Tribunal are held to be valid. At 
the same time, it also casts an onerous and responsible duty upon the persona 
designata to appoint such persons/officers as the arbitrators who are not only 
able to function independently and impartially, but are in a position to devote 
adequate time in conducting the arbitration. If the Government has nominated 
those officers as arbitrators who are not able to devote time to the arbitration 
proceedings or become incapable of acting as arbitrators because of frequent 
transfers, etc., then the principle of “default procedure” at least in the cases 
where the Government has assumed the role of appointment of arbitrators to 
itself, has to be applied in the case of substitute arbitrators as well and the 
Court will step in to appoint the arbitrator by keeping aside the procedure which

is agreed to between the parties. However, it will depend upon the facts of a

What is emphasised here is that the Court is not powerless in this regard. The 
appointment of the arbitrator by the Court, of its own choice, departing from the 
arbitration clause, is not unknown and has become an acceptable proposition of 
law which can be termed as a legal principle which has come to be established 
by a series of judgments of the Supreme Court. (Paras 17 to 19). Union of India
